a.etymology: The preposition a continues Latin ad ('to, toward, at'). It marks motion toward a destination, clock schedules (a las ocho), indirect objects, and specific human direct objects.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: a

a.notes: Before masculine singular article el, a + el contracts obligatorily into the single word al (al patio, al mediodía).

abrir.etymology: Abrir continues Latin aperīre ('to uncover, open'), with regular syncope of the unstressed internal vowel and voicing of -p- to -b- between vowels.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abrir

abrir.notes: Conjugates regularly in the present and preterite (abro, abrió), while preserving the irregular Latin-derived past participle abierto.

abuelo.etymology: The DLE traces abuelo to Vulgar Latin *aviŏlus, a diminutive built on Classical Latin avus ('grandfather, ancestor').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: abuelo

abuelo.notes: Feminine la abuela means grandmother, while plural los abuelos can refer collectively to both grandparents.

actuar.etymology: The DLE traces actuar to Medieval Latin actuare, from Latin actus. Spanish uses it both for taking action or behaving in a certain way and for performing on stage or screen.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: actuar

actuar.notes: Present-tense singular and third-person plural forms carry a written accent on ú to mark hiatus (actúo, actúa, actúan).

adorar.etymology: The DLE derives adorar from Latin adorāre. Spanish retains the religious sense of worship and also uses the verb colloquially for liking something or someone very much.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adorar

adorar.notes: Unlike gustar and encantar, adorar takes the person who feels affection as its grammatical subject (adoro el pan recién hecho).

agencia.etymology: The DLE traces agencia to Medieval Latin agentia, built on the Latin present participle agens ('one who acts or does'). Spanish uses it for a branch office or a service business such as a travel agency.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agencia

agencia.notes: Agencia is feminine (la agencia de viajes) despite containing the masculine-looking root agente.

agua.etymology: Agua descends directly from Latin aqua ('water'), showing regular Western Romance voicing of intervocalic -qu- to -gu-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agua

agua.notes: Agua is feminine, taking el in the singular solely to avoid two adjacent stressed /a/ vowels (el agua fría, las aguas claras).

ahora.etymology: Ahora developed from older agora. The DLE traces agora to the Latin phrase hac hora, meaning at this hour, so a phrase about the current hour became the everyday word for now.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ahora
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agora

ahora.notes: Ahora mismo emphasises the present moment or current situation.

al.etymology: Al is the obligatory Spanish contraction of preposition a ('to, at') + masculine singular definite article el ('the'), formed in medieval Castilian.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: al
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: a
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

al.notes: Also introduces an infinitive to express 'upon doing' (al salir de la puerta = upon stepping out the door).

alma.etymology: Alma continues Latin anĭma ('breath, life, soul'), with syncope of unstressed -i- producing Old Spanish alma through dissimilation of -nm- to -lm-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: alma

alma.notes: Like agua, feminine alma takes el in the singular before stressed initial /a/ (el alma, las almas).

anotar.etymology: Anotar comes from Latin annotāre ('to jot down, add a note to'), built from ad- + notāre (from nota, 'written mark').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: anotar

anotar.notes: Anote (formal usted command) and anota (informal tú command) are standard for jotting down a phone number or address.

aquí.etymology: The DLE derives aquí from Vulgar Latin *eccum hic ('behold here'), combining demonstrative particle eccum with Classical Latin hic ('here').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aquí

aquí.notes: Aquí points to the immediate spot right beside the speaker (aquí tiene = here you go).

ayudar.etymology: Ayudar continues Latin adiūtāre ('to help, assist'), the frequentative verb built on adiuvāre.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ayudar

ayudar.notes: Before an infinitive, ayudar links with preposition a (ayudar a llevar la maleta).

azul.etymology: Azul entered Spanish through Hispanic Arabic lazawárd, from Arabic lāzaward and Persian lāžward ('lapis lazuli'), with rebracketing of initial l- as part of the article.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: azul

azul.notes: Plural is azules; when modified by a shade word like azul oscuro ('dark blue'), the compound shade phrase stays invariable.

azúcar.etymology: Azúcar comes from Hispanic Arabic assúkkar, continuing Classical Arabic sukkar, Persian šakar, and ultimately Sanskrit śarkarā ('gravel, candied sugar crystals').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: azúcar

azúcar.notes: Commonly masculine in everyday Spain (el azúcar blanco/moreno), though the DLE accepts both masculine and feminine agreement.

año.etymology: Año descends from Latin annus. The Latin double n and the Spanish ñ give a useful visible connection between the older and modern forms of the word for a year.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: año

año.notes: Keep ñ in both año and años. The word names a period of twelve months and also occurs in the Spanish way of giving someone’s age.

barrio.etymology: The DLE derives barrio from Hispanic Arabic *bárri ('outer, suburban quarter'), from Classical Arabic barrī ('belonging to the open countryside outside town walls').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: barrio

barrio.notes: Names a distinct town neighbourhood with its own local shops, squares and daily life.

bien.etymology: Bien descends regularly from Latin bene ('well'), with stressed short Latin ĕ diphthongizing to Castilian ie and final -e dropping after -n.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bien

bien.notes: Adverbial counterpart to adjective bueno: dormir bien ('sleep well') vs un buen día ('a good day').

bizcocho.etymology: Bizcocho continues Latin bis coctus ('twice baked'), originally naming crisp ship's biscuit dried twice in the oven before shifting in Spain to light sponge cake.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bizcocho

bizcocho.notes: In Peninsula Spanish un bizcocho casero is a fluffy homemade sponge cake, often baked with lemon or cinnamon for breakfast.

blanco.etymology: Blanco entered Romance from Germanic *blank ('shining, gleaming white'), displacing Classical Latin albus as the everyday Spanish word for white.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: blanco

blanco.notes: Inflects regularly across four forms: blanco, blanca, blancos, blancas.

bollo.etymology: The DLE traces bollo ('soft bun, small roll') to Latin bulla ('bubble, rounded knob, boss'), referring to the puffed round shape of risen dough.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bollo

bollo.notes: Un bollo recién hecho in Spain is a soft sweet roll or breakfast pastry fresh from the oven.

bueno.etymology: Bueno continues Latin bonus ('good'), with stressed short Latin ŏ diphthongizing regularly to Castilian ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bueno

bueno.notes: Shortens to buen directly before a masculine singular noun (buen viaje, buen sitio), and gives the plural greeting ¡Buenos días!.

buscar.etymology: The DLE marks buscar as of uncertain pre-Roman (likely Indo-European or Celto-Romance) origin, attested early across Castilian and Portuguese.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: buscar

buscar.notes: Buscar already includes the English 'for' inside the verb: busco mis llaves (never *busco por mis llaves).

café.etymology: Café entered Spanish via French café and Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish kahve and Classical Arabic qahwah.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: café

café.notes: Names both the drink (un café con leche) and the café establishment; plural is los cafés.

caldera.etymology: Caldera continues Late Latin caldāria ('cauldron, hot-water bath'), derived from Latin calĭdus ('warm, hot').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caldera

caldera.notes: In modern buildings la caldera is the central-heating and hot-water boiler.

caliente.etymology: Caliente descends from Latin calens, calentis ('being warm or hot'), the active present participle of calēre ('to be warm').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: caliente

caliente.notes: Same singular form for masculine and feminine (té caliente, sopa caliente); diminutive calentito sounds warm and cosy.

calle.etymology: Calle continues Latin callis ('footpath, narrow track'), which broadened in Castilian to become the standard word for a paved town street.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: calle

calle.notes: Feminine noun (la calle, nuestra calle), despite ending in -e.

cama.etymology: The DLE traces cama to Late Latin cama ('low bed on the floor'), recorded by Isidore of Seville and likely of pre-Roman Hispanic origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cama

cama.notes: Hacer la cama means 'to make the bed'.

canela.etymology: Canela was borrowed from Italian cannella, diminutive of canna ('reed, small tube'), named after the rolled quill shape of dried cinnamon bark.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: canela

canela.notes: Uncountable feminine spice noun (pan con canela, una rama de canela).

carta.etymology: Carta continues Latin charta ('sheet of papyrus, written document'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek khártēs.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: carta

carta.notes: Covers a mailed letter (una carta certificada), a restaurant menu (la carta), or a playing card.

casa.etymology: Casa continues Latin casa ('cottage, hut'), which replaced Classical domus across spoken Romance as the everyday word for house and home.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: casa

casa.notes: Used without an article in en casa ('at home') and a casa ('homeward').

cerca.etymology: Cerca derives from Late Latin circa ('around, near'), used adverbially in Spanish for spatial or temporal proximity.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerca

cerca.notes: Takes de before a noun or pronoun (cerca de aquí, cerca de la estación), and stands alone at the end of a clause (está muy cerca).

cerrado.etymology: Cerrado is the participial adjective of cerrar, traced by the DLE to Late Latin serāre ('to bolt or bar a door', from sera, 'wooden bolt').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerrado
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerrar

cerrado.notes: Pairs with estar to describe whether a door, window or shop is currently shut (¿Está cerrada la puerta?).

cerrar.etymology: Cerrar continues Late Latin serāre ('to fasten with a bolt'), from Classical Latin sera ('door bar'), with initial s- assimilating to Castilian c-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cerrar

cerrar.notes: Stem-changing verb (e -> ie when stressed: cierro, cierra, cerramos).

claro.etymology: Claro continues Latin clārus ('bright, clear, distinct'). Spanish uses it for light shades of colour (azul claro), clear sound or meaning, and as a conversational affirmation ('of course!').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: claro

claro.notes: ¡Claro! and ¡Claro que sí! are everyday spoken ways to agree warmly ('of course!', 'naturally!').

clienta.etymology: Clienta is the explicit feminine counterpart created in modern Spanish from cliente (from Latin cliens, clientis) to designate a female customer or hotel guest.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cliente

clienta.notes: Both la clienta and la cliente are accepted by the RAE; la clienta is widespread in everyday Peninsula Spanish.

cliente.etymology: Cliente comes as a learned borrowing from Latin cliens, clientis ('follower, patron's protégé'), generalized in modern commerce to any customer or guest.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cliente

cliente.notes: Plural los clientes refers to guests or customers in general.

cocina.etymology: Cocina continues Late Latin coquīna ('kitchen, cooking'), derived from Classical Latin coquĕre ('to cook').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cocina

cocina.notes: Means the kitchen room, a stove/cooker, or cuisine.

coger.etymology: Coger descends from Latin colligĕre ('to gather, pick up, take hold of'), via regular syncope and palatalization in spoken Ibero-Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: coger

coger.notes: Completely standard everyday verb in Spain for taking a street, catching a train, or picking up an object (in parts of Latin America, tomar or agarrar is preferred).

como.etymology: Unaccented como develops from Vulgar Latin *quōmodo (from Classical Latin quō modo, 'in what manner'), functioning in modern Spanish for comparisons ('like, as') and causal clauses ('since').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: como

como.notes: Compare unaccented como ('like, as'; also 'I eat' from comer) with accented ¿cómo? ('how? / pardon?').

con.etymology: The preposition con continues Latin cum ('with'), marking accompaniment, ingredients (café con leche, té con miel), tools, or manner (con cuidado).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: con

con.notes: With singular personal pronouns mí, ti and reflexive sí, Latin cum fused twice to produce the special forms conmigo, contigo and consigo.

conmigo.etymology: Conmigo continues Latin mēcum ('with me'), to which Vulgar Latin re-prefixed cum (*cum mēcum > conmigo) once the final -cum was no longer felt clearly as 'with'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conmigo

conmigo.notes: Always written as one word, replacing *con mí in Spanish alongside contigo ('with you') and consigo ('with oneself').

conocer.etymology: Conocer continues Latin cognoscĕre ('to become acquainted with, recognize, know').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conocer

conocer.notes: Used for familiarity with people and places (¿Conoce usted esta calle?), whereas saber covers facts and skills.

crecer.etymology: Crecer continues Latin crescĕre. The Spanish verb covers physical growth in people and plants as well as increases in size, intensity or activity.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crecer

crecer.notes: In the first person singular present (crezco), -c- alternates with -zc- before -o, just like conocer (conozco) and parecer (parezco).

cruzar.etymology: Cruzar is formed within Romance from cruz ('cross', from Latin crux, crucis), originally meaning to lay across or pass from one side to the other.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cruzar
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cruz

cruzar.notes: Spelling changes -z- to -c- before -e (crucé el puente).

cuaderno.etymology: Cuaderno continues Late Latin quaternus ('folded sheet of four leaves', from quattuor, 'four'), how medieval notebooks and quires were bound.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuaderno

cuaderno.notes: Modern Spanish standard word for a bound notebook or exercise book.

cuarto.etymology: Cuarto descends from Latin quartus ('fourth, quarter'), developing senses for a quarter-hour (y cuarto), a fourth floor or share, and a room.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuarto

cuarto.notes: In clock time, y cuarto means quarter past and menos cuarto means quarter to (never feminine *cuarta, because cuarto here is the masculine noun 'a quarter').

cuatro.etymology: Cuatro continues Latin quattuor ('four'), with regular metathesis of final -or > -ro.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuatro

cuatro.notes: Used bare after la habitación (la habitación cuatro = Room 4) and with las for clock time (las cuatro).

cuidar.etymology: Cuidar continues Latin cōgitāre ('to think, reflect, attend carefully to'), shifting in Old Spanish from 'ponder' to 'look after, take care of'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuidar

cuidar.notes: Can take a direct object or de (cuidar las plantas / cuidar de las plantas).

de.etymology: The preposition de continues Latin dē ('from, down from, concerning'), absorbing most functions of the Latin genitive case across Romance languages.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: de

de.notes: De expresses possession (la llave de Clara), material (de madera, de latón), origin, contents (una taza de té), and part of the day after clock hours (de la mañana).

decir.etymology: Decir descends from Latin dicĕre. Its central use is putting a thought into words, and it also introduces reported speech or opinions. The modern verb shows several distinct stems, including digo, dijo and the subjunctive diga.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decir

decir.notes: Querer decir means to mean, and the polite imperative dígame is standard in Spain when answering the telephone or welcoming a customer.

dejar.etymology: The DLE traces dejar to Vulgar Latin *daxāre, altered from Classical Latin laxāre ('to loosen, release, let go') under influence of dare/delinquĕre.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dejar

dejar.notes: Covers leaving an object behind, letting someone do something, or stopping an action (dejar de + infinitive).

del.etymology: Del is the obligatory contraction of preposition de ('of, from') + masculine singular definite article el ('the').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: del
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: de
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

del.notes: Do not contract when Capitalized El belongs to a proper title or when accented pronoun él ('him') follows de (de él).

dentro.etymology: Dentro continues Latin de intro ('from within, inside'), fusing preposition de with adverb intro.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dentro

dentro.notes: Dentro de marks both spatial interior (dentro de la maleta) and time until a future event (dentro de cuarenta minutos = in forty minutes' time).

derecha.etymology: Derecha continues Late Latin directa ('straight, direct, right-hand'), feminine of directus, since the right hand was viewed as the straight or guiding hand.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: derecha
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: derecho

derecha.notes: A la derecha and a mano derecha mean 'on / to the right', whereas todo recto expresses 'straight ahead'.

desayuno.etymology: Desayuno is derived from desayunar ('to break one's fast'), built on Vulgar Latin *disieiūnāre (dis- + ieiūnāre, 'to fast').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: desayuno
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: desayunar

desayuno.notes: Literally parallel to English 'break-fast' and French déjeuner.

dibujo.etymology: Dibujo derives from dibujar ('to draw, sketch'), borrowed via Old French deboissier ('to carve or shape wood', from bois).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dibujo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dibujar

dibujo.notes: Un dibujo a lápiz is a pencil drawing or sketch.

diez.etymology: Diez descends regularly from Latin decem ('ten'), with stressed short Latin ĕ diphthongizing to ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: diez

diez.notes: Invariable numeral; diez sobre diez means 'ten out of ten'.

disculpar.etymology: Disculpar combines prefix dis- ('away') with culpar (from Latin culpa, 'fault, blame'), literally meaning 'to clear of fault or excuse'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: disculpar

disculpar.notes: Formal imperative disculpe (and plural disculpen) is a go-to polite opener in Spain for 'excuse me'.

doce.etymology: Doce continues Latin duodĕcim ('twelve', literally two + ten), reduced through Vulgar Latin *dodĕce to Old Spanish doze > doce.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: doce

doce.notes: Las doce can mean either noon or midnight; al mediodía specifies noon.

dorado.etymology: Dorado comes from dorar ('to gild'), continuing Late Latin deaurāre ('to coat with gold', from aurum, 'gold').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dorado
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dorar

dorado.notes: Describes gold-coloured metal or paper as well as golden-brown baked pastry.

dormir.etymology: Dormir continues Latin dormīre ('to sleep') with unchanged infinitive spelling.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dormir

dormir.notes: Stem vowel shifts o -> ue when stressed (duermo, duerme) and o -> u in third-person preterite (durmió, durmieron).

ducha.etymology: Ducha entered Spanish via French douche from Italian doccia ('water pipe, spout, shower'), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *ductia (from ducĕre, 'to lead or channel water').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ducha

día.etymology: Día descends from Vulgar Latin *dia, a first-declension reshaping of Classical Latin diēs ('day') that kept its original masculine gender.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: día

día.notes: Important gender exception: el día is masculine despite ending in -a (este día, ¡Buenos días!).

dónde.etymology: Accented dónde combines preposition de ('from') + onde (from Latin unde, 'whence'), generalized in Spanish to mean interrogative 'where?'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dónde
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: donde

dónde.notes: Takes a written accent in direct and indirect questions (¿Dónde está?, dime dónde está); relative donde carries no accent.

el.etymology: The definite-article family el, la and lo developed from Latin ille, illa and illud, demonstrative forms meaning that one. The old pointing forms became everyday markers of an identifiable person or thing.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

el.notes: El is the article in el mundo. It is written without the accent used by the personal pronoun él.

empezar.etymology: The DLE analyses empezar as a formation from en- and pieza. The resulting verb means to begin or start, alternating between diphthongized forms such as empiezo and unstressed-stem forms such as empezamos.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: empezar

history.meaning: the components identified by the DLE for empezar

empezar.notes: Before an infinitive, empezar always requires the preposition a (empieza a llover, empezamos a trabajar).

en.etymology: The preposition en continues Latin in ('in, inside, on'), expressing spatial containment, surface contact ('on the table' = en la mesa), and modes of transport (en tren).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: en

en.notes: Spanish uses en both where English says 'in' (en la cocina) and where English says 'on' (en la mesa, en la pared).

encantar.etymology: Encantar continues Latin incantāre ('to chant a spell over, bewitch, charm', from in- + cantāre, 'to sing').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encantar

encantar.notes: Works grammatically just like gustar: me encanta el patio (singular subject) vs me encantan las flores (plural subject).

encontrar.etymology: Encontrar derives from Late Latin incontrāre ('to meet face to face', from in + contra, 'against, opposite').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: encontrar

encontrar.notes: Stem-changing verb (o -> ue: encuentro, encuentra, encontramos).

entrar.etymology: Entrar continues Latin intrāre ('to go inside, enter'), built on adverb intra ('within').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: entrar

entrar.notes: In Spain entrar takes preposition en before a place (entrar en la posada, entrar en la cocina).

escalera.etymology: Escalera comes from Late Latin scalāria ('flight of steps'), built on Classical Latin scala ('ladder, stair').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escalera

escalera.notes: Either singular la escalera or plural las escaleras can refer to a staircase in Spanish.

escribir.etymology: Escribir continues Latin scribĕre ('to trace letters, write'), adding prosthetic initial e- before Latin impure s- + consonant.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escribir

escribir.notes: Regular across present and preterite tenses, with irregular Latin-derived past participle escrito.

escritorio.etymology: Escritorio comes as a learned derivative of Late Latin scriptōrium ('writing room, writing desk'), from scribĕre ('to write').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escritorio

escritorio.notes: Names a study or writing desk with drawers (distinct from mesa, a general table).

escuchar.etymology: Escuchar descends from Vulgar Latin *ascultāre (Classical Latin auscultāre, 'to listen attentively').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: escuchar

escuchar.notes: Like buscar and mirar, escuchar includes 'to' inside the verb: escucha la lluvia (no preposition before things).

espacio.etymology: Espacio comes from Latin spatium ('room, expanse, interval of space or time'), adding prosthetic initial e- before sp-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: espacio

esperar.etymology: Esperar continues Latin sperāre ('to hope'), expanding in Ibero-Romance to cover both 'to hope' and 'to wait for'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esperar

esperar.notes: Single Spanish verb covering English 'hope', 'expect', and 'wait for' (espero el tren = I am waiting for the train).

estación.etymology: Estación continues Latin statio, statiōnis ('standing place, post, stopping point', from stare) for both a railway station and a season of the year.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estación

estación.notes: Plural las estaciones drops the written accent because stress naturally falls on -o- before -nes.

estar.etymology: Estar comes from Latin stare, meaning to stand. In modern Spanish it expresses physical location as well as current states, conditions and resulting situations.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estar

estar.notes: Its historical association with standing does not restrict modern estar to posture: Spanish uses estar for where buildings sit (¿Dónde está la estación?) as well as temporary states (está caliente).

este.etymology: Demonstrative este continues Latin iste ('that of yours'), which shifted in Spanish to the first-person proximal demonstrative ('this, near me').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: este

este.notes: Four noun-accompanying forms: este (m sg), esta (f sg), estos (m pl, never *estes!), estas (f pl).

esto.etymology: Esto continues Latin neuter demonstrative istud ('this thing'), preserved in Spanish purely as a standalone neuter pronoun referring to an unnamed object, situation or whole idea.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esto
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: este

esto.notes: Never place neuter esto directly before a noun: masculine nouns take este (este libro) and feminine nouns take esta (esta maleta).

experto.etymology: Experto comes from Latin expertus, which the DLE glosses as experienced. Its modern uses connect practical experience with specialised skill or knowledge, and the adjective can also name an expert.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: experto

experto.notes: Experto, experta, expertos and expertas follow the person or group being described.

familia.etymology: Familia is a learned borrowing from Latin familia ('household'), preserving the Classical -li- cluster alongside inherited popular Spanish derivatives.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: familia

familia.notes: Singular collective noun taking singular verbs (su familia vivía cerca).

farmacia.etymology: Farmacia comes via Late Latin pharmacīa from Ancient Greek pharmakeía ('use or preparation of medicines', from phármakon, 'remedy').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: farmacia

farmacia.notes: Marked across Spanish streets by an illuminated green cross (la farmacia verde).

favor.etymology: Favor continues Latin favor, favōris ('goodwill, support, kindness', related to favēre, 'to show kindness').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: favor

favor.notes: Combines with por in the universal polite marker por favor ('please', literally 'out of kindness').

frío.etymology: Frío descends from Vulgar Latin *frigĭdus (Classical Latin frīgĭdus, 'cold, chill'), through loss of voiced -g- between vowels.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: frío

frío.notes: Works as an adjective (agua fría) and as a masculine noun in hace frío ('it is cold out') and tener frío ('to feel cold').

generar.etymology: Generar comes from Latin generāre, to beget or produce. Modern Spanish uses it for bringing something into existence, producing energy, or causing an effect.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: generar

generar.notes: Generar conjugates regularly across all tenses on the stem gener-.

gente.etymology: Gente descends from Latin gens, gentis. In modern Spanish it is commonly a collective word for people, so it can denote several individuals while remaining grammatically singular.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gente

gente.notes: La gente trabaja uses a singular verb. The DLE also records plural gentes; that does not make an English plural verb appropriate in every ordinary Spanish use of gente.

girar.etymology: Girar continues Late Latin gyrāre ('to turn in a circle, wheel around'), borrowed from Ancient Greek gỹros ('ring, circle').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: girar

girar.notes: Standard verb in Spain for street directions: gira a la izquierda / gira a la derecha.

gracias.etymology: Gracias is the plural of gracia, from Latin gratia ('favour, goodwill, thankfulness'; plural gratias agĕre, 'to give thanks').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gracia

gracias.notes: Always plural when thanking someone (gracias, muchas gracias); dar las gracias means 'to thank'.

grande.etymology: Grande continues Latin grandis ('large, full-grown, grand'), which largely replaced magnus across spoken Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: grande

grande.notes: Shortens to gran before any singular noun—masculine or feminine (un gran día, una gran idea)—often shifting sense toward 'great'.

guardar.etymology: Guardar entered Romance from Germanic *wardōn ('to watch over, keep safe, guard'), cognate with English ward and guard.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: guardar

guardar.notes: Everyday Spanish uses guardar for putting something away safely in a drawer, pocket or storeroom as well as keeping a secret.

gustar.etymology: Gustar continues Latin gustāre ('to taste, take a sip of'), shifting in early modern Spanish from 'someone tastes X' to 'X tastes pleasing to someone'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gustar

gustar.notes: The thing liked is the grammatical subject: me gusta el té (singular) vs me gustan los bollos (plural).

haber.etymology: Haber descends from Latin habēre, which the DLE glosses as to have. Modern Spanish uses it especially as the helper in compound tenses and in impersonal expressions of existence.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: haber

haber.notes: Ha llamado and hemos ido use haber as an auxiliary, while impersonal hay ('there is / there are') fused medieval ha + locative y ('there', from Latin ibi). Ordinary possession is expressed with tener.

habitación.etymology: Habitación comes from Latin habitātio, habitātiōnis ('dwelling, living space', from habitāre, 'to dwell').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: habitación

habitación.notes: Standard Peninsula Spanish word for a hotel room or bedroom (la habitación cuatro; plural las habitaciones).

hambre.etymology: Hambre descends from Vulgar Latin *famĭne (from Classical Latin famēs, famis, 'hunger'), via Old Spanish fambre with regular f- > silent h- and -mn- > -mbr-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hambre

hambre.notes: Feminine noun beginning with stressed /a/: singular takes el (el hambre), yet adjectives remain feminine (mucha hambre, never *mucho hambre!).

hasta.etymology: Hasta comes through Hispanic Arabic ḥattá from Classical Arabic ḥattà. The DLE also records influence from the Latin expression ad ista, meaning up to that. Its main modern use marks an endpoint in space, time or quantity.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hasta

hasta.notes: Hasta pronto is a farewell looking ahead to a future meeting.

hecho.etymology: Hecho continues Latin factus ('made, done', past participle of facĕre), showing two hallmark Castilian sound changes: initial f- > silent h- and medial -ct- > -ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hecho
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hacer

hecho.notes: Functions as past participle of hacer, adjectival recién hecho ('freshly made/baked'), and noun un hecho ('a fact').

helado.etymology: Helado continues Latin gelātus ('frozen, frosted', from gelāre, 'to freeze'), replacing initial Latin g- before e with silent h-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: helado
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: helar

helado.notes: As an adjective it means freezing cold (agua helada); as a masculine noun (un helado) it means ice cream.

hermano.etymology: Hermano descends from Latin germānus ('full brother, born of the same parents'), replacing Classical Latin frāter in Ibero-Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hermano

history.meaning: own brother / sister (of the same parents)

hermano.notes: Feminine la hermana means sister; plural los hermanos covers brothers or brothers and sisters together.

hola.etymology: The DLE classifies hola as an expressive formation and compares English hello and German hallo. It does not identify either foreign greeting as the single ancestor, so no definite borrowing chain or older root is asserted here.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hola

hola.notes: Its familiar greeting use is established. The h is not pronounced in ordinary Spanish.

hora.etymology: Hora continues Latin hōra ('hour, time of day'), borrowed from Ancient Greek hṓra ('season, hour').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hora

hora.notes: Silent h-; ¿Qué hora es? asks the clock time, while media hora means half an hour.

horrible.etymology: Horrible comes from Latin horribĭlis ('dreadful, bristling', from horrēre, 'to bristle or shudder').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: horrible

horrible.notes: Same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns (un ruido horrible, una reseña horrible).

importar.etymology: Importar comes from Latin importāre ('to bring in, carry weight, be of consequence'), developing both commercial ('import') and evaluative ('matter, mind') uses.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: importar

importar.notes: In ¿No le importa...? ('Do you mind...?') and No importa ('It doesn't matter'), importar takes indirect object pronouns like gustar.

ir.etymology: The infinitive ir comes from Latin ire, meaning to go. Modern ir is highly irregular and also works with another verb to express motion, a future action or a gradually developing process.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ir

ir.notes: In hemos ido creciendo, ido is the past participle of ir. The expression describes gradual growth; it does not describe a journey.

izquierda.etymology: Izquierda was borrowed into medieval Castilian from Basque ezkerra ('the left hand, left-handed'), displacing inherited Latin sinister.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: izquierda
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: izquierdo

izquierda.notes: One of Spanish's most famous Basque loanwords; a la izquierda means 'on / to the left'.

junto.etymology: Junto continues Latin iunctus ('joined, linked together', past participle of iungĕre, 'to yoke or join').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: junto

junto.notes: Plural juntos/juntas means 'together' agreeing with the subjects, while invariable junto a + noun means 'next to / beside'.

justo.etymology: Justo descends from Latin iustus ('fair, exact, rightful', from ius, 'law, right').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: justo

justo.notes: Used adverbially before location or time phrases to mean 'right / exact' (justo al lado de la cama = right next to the bed).

la.etymology: Both feminine singular article la ('the') and feminine direct-object pronoun la ('her, it') continue unstressed Latin illa / illam ('that').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: la
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

la.notes: In clock time, singular la una ('one o'clock') contrasts with plural las dos, las tres...

lado.etymology: Lado continues Latin latus ('flank, side'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to Castilian -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lado

lado.notes: Al lado de ('next to, beside') and al lado ('on the side / next door') are core spatial building blocks.

las.etymology: Las continues Latin feminine accusative plural illās ('those'), serving as both the feminine plural definite article ('the') and direct-object pronoun ('them').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: la
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

las.notes: Used before numbers 2–12 to express clock hours (son las ocho, a las siete y media), agreeing with implied horas.

le.etymology: Indirect-object pronoun le continues Latin dative singular illī ('to him, to her, to that one').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: le

le.notes: Covers 'to him', 'to her', and formal 'to you' (usted); changes to se when followed immediately by lo, la, los or las.

leche.etymology: Leche descends from Vulgar Latin *lacte (Classical Latin lac, lactis, 'milk'), with the Latin -ct- cluster palatalizing regularly to Castilian -ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: leche

leche.notes: Feminine noun in Spanish (la leche fría, café con leche), unlike masculine French lait and Italian latte.

leer.etymology: Leer continues Latin legĕre ('to gather, pick out letters, read'), with loss of voiced palatalized -g- between vowels.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: leer

leer.notes: Unstressed -i- turns to -y- between vowels in preterite third-person forms (leyó, leyeron) and gerund leyendo.

les.etymology: Les continues Latin dative plural illīs ('to them'), marking plural indirect objects ('to them' or formal plural 'to you all', ustedes).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: le

les.notes: Like singular le, les turns into se before direct-object pronouns lo, la, los, las.

libro.etymology: Libro continues Latin liber, librī ('inner bark of a tree, scroll, book').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: libro

libro.notes: El libro de reservas is a hotel's reservation ledger.

limonero.etymology: Limonero adds the Spanish fruit-tree suffix -ero (from Latin -ārius) to limón ('lemon') to name the lemon tree.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: limonero
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: limón

limonero.notes: Many Spanish fruit trees pair a feminine or masculine fruit with a masculine -ero tree: limón -> limonero, naranja -> naranjo/naranjero, manzana -> manzano.

limpio.etymology: Limpio descends from Latin limpĭdus ('clear, transparent, pure'), shifting in Ibero-Romance to the everyday adjective for 'clean'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: limpio

limpio.notes: Note the difference in stress between adjective limpio (ˈlimpjo, 'clean') and preterite verb limpió (limˈpjo, 'cleaned').

limón.etymology: Limón entered Spanish through Hispanic Arabic laymún, from Classical Arabic laymūn and Persian līmūn ('citrus fruit, lemon').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: limón

limón.notes: Drops its written accent in the plural: los limones.

llamar.etymology: Llamar continues Latin clamāre, to call out, with initial Latin cl- palatalizing regularly into Castilian ll-. Present-day senses include calling out, telephoning, knocking or ringing, and naming.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: llamar

llamar.notes: Reflexive llamarse expresses someone's name (¿Cómo se llama usted?, Me llamo Clara).

llave.etymology: Llave descends regularly from Latin clāvis ('key'), illustrating Castilian palatalization of initial Latin cl- > ll- (compare llamar < clamāre, lluvia < pluvia).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: llave

llave.notes: Feminine noun: la llave, las llaves; llave inglesa ('English key') means an adjustable spanner/wrench.

llevar.etymology: Llevar continues Latin levāre, meaning to raise or lift. Its modern meanings extend to carrying items, wearing clothes, managing affairs, and expressing how long a situation has lasted.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: llevar

llevar.notes: Llevar + time expression (llevo dos días aquí) states how long someone has been doing something without needing a perfect tense.

lluvia.etymology: Lluvia continues Latin pluvia ('rain'), with initial Latin pl- palatalizing regularly to Castilian ll-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lluvia

lluvia.notes: Paired with verb llover ('to rain', stem-changing: llueve = it is raining).

lo.etymology: Lo continues Latin accusative illum (masculine) and neuter illud ('that'). In modern Spanish it serves both as the masculine singular direct-object pronoun ('him, it') and as the neuter article before adjectives (lo importante, lo que necesitas).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lo

lo.notes: Lo que ('what / the thing that') opens headless relative clauses when no specific masculine or feminine noun has been named.

los.etymology: Los continues Latin masculine accusative plural illōs ('those'), serving as both masculine plural definite article ('the') and direct-object pronoun ('them').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lo

los.notes: Los dos means 'both of them'; los lunes means 'on Mondays'.

luego.etymology: Luego descends from Latin locō (ablative of locus, 'on the spot, immediately'), which shifted in Spanish from 'right away' to 'then, afterwards, later'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: luego

luego.notes: ¡Hasta luego! ('See you later!') is Spain's most frequent everyday goodbye.

lunes.etymology: Lunes continues Late Latin (diēs) Lūnae ('Moon's day'), adding final analogical -s on the model of martes, miércoles, jueves and viernes.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lunes

lunes.notes: All weekdays ending in unstressed -es keep the same spelling in the plural: el lunes ('on Monday'), los lunes ('on Mondays').

lámpara.etymology: Lámpara comes from Latin lampas, lampădis ('torch, oil lamp', from Ancient Greek lampás), with dissimilation of -d- to -r- in Ibero-Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lámpara

lámpara.notes: Carries proparoxytonic (esdrújula) stress on its first syllable, always marked with a written accent: lám-pa-ra.

mal.etymology: The adverb mal continues Latin male ('badly, ill'), while the noun el mal ('harm, illness') and apocopated adjective mal before masculine singular nouns connect to malo (from Latin malus).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mal

mal.notes: Menos mal ('thank goodness' / 'just as well') is one of everyday Peninsula Spanish's most common expressions of relief.

maleta.etymology: The DLE traces maleta ('suitcase') to Old French malete, diminutive of male ('travelling bag, leather pouch', from Frankish *malha).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: maleta

maleta.notes: Hacer la maleta means 'to pack one's suitcase'.

mano.etymology: Mano continues fourth-declension Latin manus ('hand'), preserving its original Latin feminine gender despite ending in -o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mano

mano.notes: Classic gender exception: la mano, las manos, esta mano, a mano derecha ('on the right-hand side').

mantequilla.etymology: Mantequilla builds a Spanish diminutive (-illa) on manteca ('lard, fat', a pre-Roman Hispanic word) to designate churned cow's-milk butter.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mantequilla
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: manteca

mantequilla.notes: Standard word for butter in Spain and most of the Spanish-speaking world.

mañana.etymology: Mañana derives from Vulgar Latin *(hora) maneāna ('early morning hour', from Latin māne, 'in the morning').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mañana

mañana.notes: Feminine la mañana means 'the morning' (por la mañana, ¡Hasta mañana!), whereas adverbial mañana with no article means 'tomorrow'.

me.etymology: The unstressed pronoun me continues Latin accusative me (with dative mihi merging in Vulgar Latin), marking the speaker as direct object, indirect object, or reflexive participant.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: me

me.notes: Unstressed me stands before finite verbs (me encanta, me llamo) and attaches to the end of infinitives, gerunds and affirmative imperatives (dígame, déjame).

medio.etymology: Medio continues Latin medius ('middle, half'), inflecting as an adjective for 'half' (media hora, a las siete y media).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: medio

medio.notes: In clock time y media is feminine because it agrees with implied media hora ('half an hour').

mediodía.etymology: Mediodía fuses medio ('middle') + día ('day') on the pattern of Latin merīdiēs ('midday, noon').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mediodía

mediodía.notes: Masculine singular compound noun: al mediodía means 'at noon'.

mesa.etymology: Mesa continues Latin mēnsa ('table'), with early spoken Latin loss of -n- before -s- (*mēsa).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mesa

mesa.notes: Poner la mesa means 'to set the table'.

mi.etymology: Unstressed possessive determiner mi ('my') developed as the proclitic shortening of Old Spanish mío/mía (from Latin meus, mea) before a singular noun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mi

mi.notes: Same form before masculine and feminine nouns (mi hermano, mi maleta); plural adds -s (mis llaves). No accent, unlike prepositional mí.

mirar.etymology: Mirar continues Latin mīrārī ('to wonder at, gaze in admiration'), weakening in Romance to the ordinary active verb 'to look at, watch'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mirar

mirar.notes: Imperatives mira (tú), mire (usted) and mirad (vosotros) are constantly used in conversation to draw attention ('look!').

mismo.etymology: The DLE reconstructs Vulgar Latin *metipsĭmus behind mismo. It combines the emphatic element -met with a superlative of Latin ipse, meaning the same. The asterisk marks the reconstructed form.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mismo

history.meaning: an intensified form related to the same

mismo.notes: Mismo still expresses identity or emphasis. In ahora mismo it reinforces the time expression rather than agreeing with a person.

modelo.etymology: Modelo was borrowed from Italian modello. The DLE takes that word back through reconstructed Vulgar Latin *modellus to Latin modŭlus, associated with measure or a measured rhythm. The asterisk identifies the reconstructed stage.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: modelo

history.meaning: a diminutive formation behind Italian modello

modelo.notes: Spanish uses modelo both for a pattern to copy and for a person who models. A person can be el modelo or la modelo.

mostrador.etymology: Mostrador derives from mostrar ('to show, display', from Latin monstrāre) + instrument/place suffix -dor: originally a shop counter where goods were laid out to show customers.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mostrador
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mostrar

mostrador.notes: Standard Spanish word for a hotel reception desk, café bar counter, or shop counter.

muchísimo.etymology: Muchísimo combines mucho (from Latin multus) with the learned superlative suffix -ísimo (from Latin -issĭmus) to express 'very much' or 'a great deal'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mucho
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -ísimo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: mucho

muchísimo.notes: Muchísimo inflects as an adjective before nouns (muchísimas gracias) and stays invariable as an adverb after verbs.

morphemes.meaning: large amount or degree, from mucho

mundo.etymology: Mundo continues Latin mundus. The DLE describes the world sense of that Latin word as a semantic calque of Greek kósmos: the meaning was modelled on the Greek expression rather than its sound being borrowed.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mundo

mundo.notes: Todo el mundo uses world collectively for everyone and takes a singular verb.

muy.etymology: Muy is a shortened form of older muito, which continues Latin multum. The DLE also identifies it as a reduced form of mucho; this older family therefore supplies both very and much in modern Spanish.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: muy
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mucho

muy.notes: In muy claro it raises the degree of clear. It does not change for the number or gender of the people involved.

más.etymology: Más developed through the older form maes from Latin magis. The modern word expresses a greater quantity or degree and can also intensify a comparison.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: más

más.notes: Más de before a number sets a threshold: más de veinticinco means more than twenty-five.

mí.etymology: Mí continues Latin dative pronoun mihi ('to me'). In modern Spanish it survives as the stressed first-person singular pronoun used after prepositions (para mí, cerca de mí).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mí
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: yo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: me

mí.notes: The written accent distinguishes prepositional pronoun mí ('me') from unaccented possessive determiner mi ('my').

nadie.etymology: Nadie evolved from Old Spanish nadi, continuing the Latin plural phrase (homĭnēs) nātī ('people born', i.e. 'any living soul') used in negative clauses.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nadie

nadie.notes: Stands alone before the verb (Nadie dice que no) or pairs with no before the verb (No hay nadie).

negro.etymology: Negro continues Latin niger, nigra, nigrum ('glossy black, dark'), with short Latin ĭ lowering regularly to Castilian e.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: negro

negro.notes: Té negro is black tea; for black espresso coffee in Spain, speakers normally say un café solo.

nevera.etymology: Nevera derives from nieve ('snow', from Latin nix, nivis) + place suffix -era: historically an icehouse packed with mountain snow to preserve food, now the household refrigerator.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nevera
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nieve

nevera.notes: La nevera (alongside el frigorífico) is the everyday Peninsula Spanish word for fridge.

no.etymology: No continues Latin nōn ('not'). In Spanish it serves both as the standalone negative answer ('no') and as the preverbal negator placed directly before the verb phrase.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: no

no.notes: When negative words like nadie or nada follow the verb, no still precedes the verb (No hay nadie en el patio).

noche.etymology: Noche descends regularly from Latin nox, noctis ('night'), showing palatalization of medial -ct- > -ch- (compare leche < *lacte, ocho < octo).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: noche

noche.notes: Esta noche means 'tonight', anoche means 'last night', and ¡Buenas noches! serves as both 'good evening' after dark and 'good night'.

nos.etymology: Unstressed object and reflexive pronoun nos ('us, to us, ourselves') continues Latin accusative/dative nōs unchanged.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nos

nos.notes: Also marks reciprocal action: ¡Nos vemos! ('See you!', literally 'we see each other') and nos tuteamos ('we use tú with each other').

nosotros.etymology: Nosotros fused Old Spanish nos ('we', from Latin nōs) with otros ('others', from Latin altĕrōs), originally contrasting 'we ourselves (as opposed to others)' before becoming the standard subject pronoun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nosotros

nosotros.notes: Feminine nosotras is used when an all-female group speaks of itself.

nuestro.etymology: Nuestro continues Vulgar Latin *noster, nostra, nostrum ('our, ours'), showing diphthongization of short stressed ŏ to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nuestro

nuestro.notes: Agrees in gender and number with the thing possessed (nuestro barrio, nuestra puerta, nuestros clientes).

nueve.etymology: Nueve descends from Latin novem ('nine'), with stressed short ŏ diphthongizing regularly to Castilian ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nueve

nuevo.etymology: Nuevo continues Latin novus ('new, fresh, recent'), diphthongizing stressed short ŏ to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nuevo

nuevo.notes: De nuevo means 'again' (¡Buenos días de nuevo! = Good morning again!).

o.etymology: The conjunction o ('or') continues Latin aut ('or'), with Latin au monophthongizing regularly to Castilian o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: o

o.notes: Changes spelling and sound to u before words starting with /o/ (o- or ho-, e.g. siete u ocho).

ocho.etymology: Ocho descends regularly from Latin octō ('eight'), with medial -ct- palatalizing to Castilian -ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ocho

ocho.notes: Las ocho en punto means 'eight o'clock sharp'.

oficio.etymology: Oficio continues Latin officium, duty, service or function. Spanish uses it for a skilled trade or craft learned through practice as well as an official duty or occupation.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oficio

oficio.notes: Compare el oficio (a skilled craft or trade) with la oficina (an office room or workplace).

once.etymology: Once continues Latin undĕcim ('eleven', literally one + ten) via Vulgar Latin *undĕce > Old Spanish onze > once.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: once

once.notes: Las once y veinte means 'eleven twenty'.

ordenador.etymology: Ordenador ('computer' in Spain) was adapted from French ordinateur (coined in 1955 from Latin ordinātor, 'one who puts things in order', from ordināre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ordenador

ordenador.notes: Standard word for computer across Spain (while computadora or computador is used in Latin America).

oír.etymology: Oír continues Latin audīre ('to hear'), with au > o and loss of intervocalic -d- leaving a two-syllable hiatus marked by the accent on -ír.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oír

oír.notes: Irregular present stem oigo, oyes, oye, oímos, oís, oyen; ¡Oye! / ¡Oiga! is a common way to get someone's attention.

pan.etymology: Pan continues Latin pānis ('bread, loaf'), dropping final unstressed -e after -n in singular Castilian.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pan

para.etymology: Para developed from Old Spanish pora, fusing Latin pro ('for, on behalf of') + ad ('to, toward') to express destination, recipient, deadline and purpose.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: para

para.notes: Followed directly by an infinitive, para expresses 'in order to' (para abrir la puerta).

pasar.etymology: Pasar derives from Vulgar Latin *passāre ('to take steps, pass through'), built on Classical Latin passus ('step, pace').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pasar

pasar.notes: Covers walking past a landmark, handing something over (pásame la llave), spending time, happening (¿Qué pasa?), and welcoming someone inside (¡Pase usted!).

patio.etymology: The DLE marks patio ('inner courtyard') as of uncertain origin, likely through Occitan or Catalan pati from a Vulgar Latin derivative of patēre ('to lie open to the sky').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: patio

patio.notes: Heart of traditional Spanish town buildings, bringing daylight, lemon trees and fresh air to surrounding galleries.

pedir.etymology: Pedir continues Latin petĕre ('to head for, seek, request'), shifting to the -ir conjugation with regular voicing of -t- > -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pedir

pedir.notes: Stem vowel alternates e -> i (pido, pide, pidió); pedir means to request or order (whereas preguntar means to ask a question).

pequeño.etymology: The DLE traces pequeño ('small, little, young') to an expressive Ibero-Romance *pikk- / *pett- root for tiny things (compare Italian piccolo and French petit).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pequeño

pequeño.notes: Used as an adjective (una calle pequeña) or noun for a young child (el pequeño = the younger boy).

perdonar.etymology: Perdonar continues Medieval Latin perdonāre ('to grant wholeheartedly, remit a debt, forgive', from per- + donāre, 'to give').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: perdonar

perdonar.notes: Imperative perdona (tú) or perdone (usted) is a polite everyday way to get someone's attention ('excuse me').

perdón.etymology: Perdón is the deverbal noun of perdonar (from Medieval Latin perdonāre), used standalone as an immediate apology ('sorry! / pardon me!').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: perdón
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: perdonar

perdón.notes: Perdón por el retraso / perdón por el error means 'sorry for the delay / mistake'.

pero.etymology: The conjunction pero comes from Latin per hoc, meaning because of or through this. Its modern contrastive use introduces a qualification or a different point after the first part of a statement.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pero

pero.notes: The conjunction is a different dictionary entry from the unrelated fruit name pero.

piedra.etymology: Piedra continues Latin petra ('rock, stone', borrowed from Ancient Greek pétra), with stressed short ĕ diphthongizing to ie and -tr- voicing to -dr-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: piedra

piedra.notes: De piedra ('made of stone', e.g. el puente de piedra) links material with de.

planta.etymology: Planta continues Latin planta ('sprout, shoot; sole of the foot'), extending from a living plant and ground footprint to each storey or floor of a building.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: planta

planta.notes: In Spain la planta baja is the ground floor, la primera planta is one flight up, and la segunda planta is two flights up.

plaza.etymology: Plaza descends from Vulgar Latin *plattea (Classical Latin platēa, 'broad street, courtyard', from Greek plateîa, 'wide way').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plaza

plaza.notes: Diminutive la placita names a small, intimate neighbourhood square.

poco.etymology: Poco descends regularly from Latin paucus ('few, little'), with Latin au monophthongizing to Castilian o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poco

poco.notes: Un poco de ('a little bit of') stays masculine singular even before feminine uncountable nouns (un poco de leche, un poco de agua).

poder.etymology: Poder evolved from Vulgar Latin *potēre, regularizing Classical Latin posse ('to be able, have power').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poder

poder.notes: Followed directly by an infinitive without any preposition (¿Puede ayudarme?, no puedo abrirla).

poner.etymology: Poner continues Latin pōnĕre ('to place, put, set down'), shifting to the Spanish second conjugation.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner

poner.notes: Irregular forms include pongo (1sg present), pon (tú command), puse/puso (preterite), and puesto (past participle).

por.etymology: Por merges Latin pro ('on behalf of, in exchange for, because of') and per ('through, along, by means of') into a single versatile Spanish preposition.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: por

por.notes: Marks parts of the day (por la mañana, por la tarde), movement through space (por el puente, por la escalera), and cause or motive (por favor).

posada.etymology: Posada derives from posar ('to lodge, rest, set down one's load', from Late Latin pausāre, 'to pause, halt for rest').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: posada
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: posar

posada.notes: Historically a traditional Spanish coaching inn where travellers paused for lodging and meals.

pronto.etymology: Pronto continues Latin promptus. The Spanish word can refer to readiness or speed and also functions as an adverb for an early or near-future time.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pronto

pronto.notes: Hasta pronto means see you soon; pronto does not describe the person’s character in this farewell.

puente.etymology: Puente continues Latin pons, pontis ('bridge'), diphthongizing stressed short ŏ to Castilian ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: puente

puente.notes: Masculine in modern standard Spanish: el puente de piedra, cruzar el puente.

puerta.etymology: Puerta descends regularly from Latin porta ('city gate, doorway, door'), with stressed short ŏ diphthongizing to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: puerta

puerta.notes: Covers both a room's door and the main street entrance or gate of a building.

punto.etymology: Punto continues Latin punctum ('prick, dot, exact point in space or time', from pungĕre, 'to pierce').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: punto

punto.notes: En punto after a clock hour means 'on the dot / sharp' (a las ocho en punto); estar a punto de + infinitive means 'to be about to'.

que.etymology: Unaccented que continues unstressed Latin quid and quem, merging relative pronoun ('who, which, that') and subordinating conjunction ('that, than') into one high-frequency connector.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: que

que.notes: Unaccented que connects clauses (creo que sí, más que ayer), whereas accented qué asks direct or indirect questions (¿Qué hora es?).

quedar.etymology: Quedar continues Latin quiētāre ('to rest, become still', from quiētus), shifting in Spanish to 'stay, remain, be left, or arrange to meet'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: quedar

quedar.notes: Reflexive quedarse means 'to stay' (me quedo toda la semana), non-reflexive quedar means 'to be left' or 'to meet up' (quedar al mediodía).

querer.etymology: Querer continues Latin quaerĕre, which the DLE glosses as seeking or asking. Modern Spanish uses querer both for wanting something and for feeling affection toward a person.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: querer

querer.notes: With a person introduced by a (querer a alguien), querer expresses love or affection; before a noun or infinitive (quiero un café, queremos descansar), it expresses a wish.

qué.etymology: Interrogative and exclamative qué continues stressed Latin quid ('what?'), written with an acute accent to distinguish it from unstressed conjunction/relative que.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: qué

qué.notes: Used in questions (¿Qué hora es?, ¿Qué pasa?) and exclamations before nouns or adjectives/adverbs (¡Qué alivio!, ¡Qué bien!).

razón.etymology: Razón continues Latin ratio, ratiōnis ('reckoning, calculation, reason, rightness').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: razón

razón.notes: Feminine noun (la razón, las razones); tener razón means 'to be right' (literally 'to have reason').

recepcionista.etymology: Recepcionista combines recepción (from Latin receptio, 'welcoming, receiving') with agent suffix -ista (from Greek -istēs via Latin -ista).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recepcionista
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recepción

recepcionista.notes: Like all -ista person nouns, recepcionista keeps the same spelling for both genders: el recepcionista / la recepcionista.

recién.etymology: Recién is the apocopated adverbial form of reciente ('recent, fresh', from Latin recens, recentis), used directly before past participles.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recién
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reciente

recién.notes: In Spain recién pairs chiefly with past participles: bollos recién hechos ('freshly baked buns'), café recién hecho ('freshly brewed coffee').

recto.etymology: Recto comes as a learned borrowing from Latin rectus ('straight, upright, direct', past participle of regĕre, 'to guide straight').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: recto

recto.notes: Todo recto ('straight ahead') is the standard Peninsula Spanish phrase when giving walking directions.

reloj.etymology: Reloj entered Old Spanish via Old Catalan relotge from Latin horologium ('time-teller, sundial, clock', from Ancient Greek hōrológion).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reloj

reloj.notes: Covers both a wall/church clock and a wristwatch; plural adds -es: los relojes.

representante.etymology: Representante is formed from representar and the ending -nte. The base verb continues Latin repraesentāre, and the ending historically comes from Latin active present participles. A representative is someone who performs the action of representing.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: representante
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: representar
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -nte

representante.notes: For a talent agent, the DLE specifies managing artists’ contracts and professional affairs. The person noun can take el or la without changing representante.

reserva.etymology: Reserva is the deverbal noun of reservar, from Latin reservāre ('to keep back, save for someone', from re- + servāre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reserva
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reservar

reserva.notes: Tengo una reserva a nombre de... ('I have a reservation under the name of...') is the key hotel check-in phrase.

reseña.etymology: Reseña derives from reseñar ('to record identifying marks, review'), continuing Latin resignāre / *risignāre (built on signum, 'mark, sign').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reseña
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: reseñar

history.meaning: note down marks -> review; brief report

reseña.notes: Today una reseña covers book reviews as well as online guest reviews of hotels and cafés.

rojo.etymology: Rojo descends from Latin russus ('deep red, russet'), displacing older Castilian bermejo and colorado as the standard basic term for red.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: rojo

rojo.notes: Regular four-form colour adjective: rojo, roja, rojos, rojas.

saber.etymology: Saber continues Latin sapĕre ('to have a flavour, taste; be discerning, know'), preserving BOTH senses in modern Spanish ('to know' and 'to taste like').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: saber

history.meaning: taste; have wisdom -> know; taste of

saber.notes: Irregular 1sg sé ('I know'); saber a + noun means 'to taste like' (sabe a canela = it tastes like cinnamon).

salir.etymology: Salir continues Latin salīre ('to leap, spring forth'), shifting in Ibero-Romance to the general verb for going out, leaving or departing.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: salir

salir.notes: Irregular 1sg present salgo and imperative sal; takes preposition de for leaving a place (salir de la posada).

salvar.etymology: Salvar continues Late Latin salvāre ('to make safe, rescue, save', from Classical Latin salvus, 'safe, unharmed').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: salvar

salvar.notes: Covers rescuing people or objects and figuratively 'saving the day' (salvar el desayuno).

seguir.etymology: Seguir descends from Vulgar Latin *sequīre (Classical deponent sequī, 'to follow, continue along').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: seguir

seguir.notes: Drops silent u before -o/-a (sigo) and changes stem vowel e -> i (sigue, siguió); sigue todo recto means 'keep going straight ahead'.

semana.etymology: Semana continues Late Latin septimāna ('period of seven days', from septem, 'seven').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: semana

semana.notes: Toda la semana means 'all week', and la semana que viene means 'next week'.

sentar.etymology: Sentar derives from Vulgar Latin *sedentāre ('to seat, cause to sit'), built on Latin sedens, sedentis (present participle of sedēre, 'to sit').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: sentar

sentar.notes: Reflexive sentarse means 'to sit down'; polite command siéntese attaches -se and adds a written accent to keep stress on sién-.

ser.etymology: The DLE traces the modern infinitive to older seer, whose entry gives Latin sedēre, meaning to sit. This is the history of the infinitive; the highly irregular modern conjugation cannot be explained by treating all its forms as regular changes to that one stem.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ser
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: seer

ser.notes: Soy and somos belong to ser even though neither contains the letters ser. Use the conjugation table for the present-day forms.

servir.etymology: Servir continues Latin servīre ('to serve, be useful, wait at table').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: servir

servir.notes: Stem-changing verb (e -> i: sirvo, sirve, sirvió); ¿Para qué sirve? asks 'What is it used for?'.

señor.etymology: Señor continues Latin senior, seniōris ('older, elder', comparative of senex), which became a feudal title of respect across Romance ('lord, sir, gentleman').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: señor

señor.notes: Takes definite article el when speaking about someone (el señor Gómez), and no article when addressing someone directly (¡Buenos días, señor!).

señora.etymology: Señora was formed in medieval Spanish by adding feminine -a to señor (from Latin seniōrem) as the respectful title 'madam, Mrs, lady'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: señor
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: señora

señora.notes: Polite address in hospitality: pase por aquí, señora ('right this way, ma'am').

siempre.etymology: Siempre descends regularly from Latin semper ('always, at all times'), with stressed short ĕ diphthongizing to ie and final -er metathesizing to -re.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: siempre

siempre.notes: Siempre que + subjunctive means 'whenever / provided that'.

siete.etymology: Siete continues Latin septem ('seven'), with stressed short ĕ diphthongizing to ie and medial -pt- simplifying to -t-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: siete

siete.notes: Combines in plural setent- (setenta = 70) and ordinal séptimo ('seventh').

silla.etymology: Silla descends regularly from Latin sella ('seat, chair, saddle', related to sedēre), with stressed short ĕ before palatalized -ll- raising to Castilian -i-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: silla

silla.notes: Contrast la silla (individual chair with a backrest) with el sillón (armchair).

sobre.etymology: Preposition sobre ('on, upon, about') continues Latin super ('above, over'); noun el sobre ('envelope') arose as a clipping of sobrescrito ('address written on the outside cover').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: sobre

sobre.notes: Homograph pair in Spanish: preposition sobre ('on / about / out of') and masculine noun un sobre blanco ('a white envelope').

sol.etymology: Sol continues Latin sōl, sōlis ('sun') with unchanged spelling.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: sol

su.etymology: Unstressed possessive determiner su ('his, her, its, their, your [usted/ustedes]') reduced in Old Spanish from suyo/suya (from Latin suus, sua).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: su

history.meaning: one's own -> his / her / their / your (formal)

su.notes: Agrees only in number with the noun possessed (su llave, sus llaves), never with the owner.

subir.etymology: Subir continues Latin subīre ('to go under, mount from below, climb up', from sub- + īre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: subir

subir.notes: Works both intransitively ('go upstairs': suba por aquí) and transitively ('carry upstairs': yo subo la maleta).

tarde.etymology: Tarde continues Latin tardē ('slowly, late'), serving both as an adverb ('late') and as the feminine noun la tarde ('the afternoon / early evening').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tarde

tarde.notes: In Spain la tarde stretches from lunch until nightfall (roughly 2 p.m. to 8 or 9 p.m.), greeted with ¡Buenas tardes!.

tarjeta.etymology: Tarjeta was borrowed as a diminutive from French targette / Italian targhetta ('small shield, plaque, name-card', from Germanic *targa, 'shield').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tarjeta

tarjeta.notes: Covers a luggage tag (una tarjeta de cartón), business card, postcard, or payment card (con tarjeta).

taza.etymology: Taza entered Spanish through Hispanic Arabic ṭássa, from Arabic ṭassah and Persian tašt ('small bowl, cup').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: taza

taza.notes: Una taza has a handle for hot drinks like tea or coffee, whereas un vaso is a drinking glass.

te.etymology: Unstressed pronoun te ('you, to you, yourself' for informal singular tú) continues Latin accusative tē unchanged.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: te

te.notes: Unaccented pronoun te contrasts with accented noun el té ('tea').

teléfono.etymology: Teléfono came via French téléphone, built from Greek tēle- ('far off') + phōnē ('voice, sound').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: teléfono

teléfono.notes: Proparoxytonic stress on -lé- requires the written accent: el teléfono.

tener.etymology: Tener continues Latin tenēre, historically meaning to hold or grasp. Over time tener replaced haber as the ordinary Spanish verb of possession and took on many everyday idioms of state and obligation.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tener

tener.notes: Spanish uses tener + noun for states where English uses 'be' + adjective: tener razón (be right), tener hambre (be hungry), tener frío (be cold), and tener prisa (be in a hurry).

tercero.etymology: Tercero derives from Latin tertiārius ('containing a third, third in order', built on tertius, 'third').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tercero

tercero.notes: Shortens to tercer before a masculine singular noun (el tercer día), while staying full in feminine la tercera planta.

timbre.etymology: Timbre came into Spanish via Old French timbre ('small bell struck with a hammer'), from Latin tympănum ('drum, tambourine', from Greek týmpanon).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: timbre

timbre.notes: Names a doorbell, a hotel reception desk bell (tocar el timbre), an ink seal, or vocal tone.

todavía.etymology: Todavía fused toda + vía (from Latin tōta via, 'all the way, continually'), shifting from 'always' in medieval Spanish to 'still' (affirmative) and 'yet' (with no).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: todavía

todavía.notes: Todavía está caliente means 'it is still warm', while ¿Todavía no? means 'Not yet?'.

todo.etymology: Todo comes from Latin totus, meaning whole or entire. Spanish uses this inherited word both for a complete whole and for all the members of a group.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: todo

todo.notes: In todo el mundo the complete world stands for everyone. Todo follows the singular masculine mundo even though many people are meant.

tomar.etymology: The DLE marks tomar ('to take; to have food or drink') as of uncertain Hispanic origin (variously linked to Latin autumāre or an expressive root).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tomar

tomar.notes: Most natural Spanish verb for ordering or having a drink or snack: ¿Qué va a tomar?, tomo un té con miel.
