trabajar.etymology: The DLE traces trabajar to reconstructed Vulgar Latin *tripaliāre, associated with torture, and ultimately to Late Latin tripalium, a three-timber instrument of torture. The asterisk marks an inferred historical form rather than an attested spelling.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: trabajar

trabajar.notes: Modern trabajar covers physical or intellectual activity, paid employment and practising a profession. Those present-day meanings should be learned in their own contexts.

tranquilo.etymology: Tranquilo comes as a learned borrowing from Latin tranquillus ('calm, still, peaceful').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tranquilo

tranquilo.notes: Used both to describe quiet places (un patio tranquilo) and to reassure people ('don't worry / take it easy': ¡Tranquilo!).

tratar.etymology: Tratar comes from Latin tractāre. The Spanish word covers handling or managing something, dealing with people, and discussing a subject. With de and an infinitive it can express an attempt.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tratar

tratar.notes: Tratamos de trabajar means we try to work. The following de is part of that construction.

tren.etymology: Tren entered Spanish from French train ('line of carriages pulled together', from Old French traïner, 'to draw or haul along').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tren

tren.notes: Plural adds -es: el tren, los trenes; viajar en tren means 'to travel by train'.

tu.etymology: Unstressed possessive determiner tu ('your', singular informal) shortened from Old Spanish tuyo/tuya, continuing Latin tuus, tua.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tu

tu.notes: Written without an accent before nouns (tu caja, tus llaves), distinct from accented subject pronoun tú ('you').

tubería.etymology: Tubería builds collective suffix -ería on tubo ('pipe, tube', from Latin tubus, 'water pipe, conduit') to designate plumbing or a water pipe.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tubería
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tubo

tubería.notes: Carries a hiatus accent on -í-: la tubería.

tutear.etymology: Tutear is formed inside Spanish from pronoun tú + frequentative verbal suffix -ear: literally 'to address someone as tú'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tutear
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tú

tutear.notes: Reciprocal ¿Nos tuteamos? ('Shall we use tú with each other?') is how Spanish speakers invite first-name informality.

té.etymology: Té entered European languages through seventeenth-century maritime trade from Hokkien Chinese tê ('tea', compare Mandarin chá).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: té

té.notes: Always carries a written accent (el té, plural los tés) to distinguish it from unaccented pronoun te ('you').

tú.etymology: Subject pronoun tú ('you', singular informal) continues Latin nominative tū unchanged in sound, adding a written accent in Spanish orthography.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tú

tú.notes: The written accent distinguishes subject pronoun tú ('you') from possessive determiner tu ('your').

un.etymology: Un is the shortened form associated with uno and una. The DLE derives that family from Latin unus. The numeral for one also supplies the Spanish indefinite article used before a singular count noun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: un
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: uno

un.notes: Un oficio means a profession. The shortened form un normally appears before a masculine singular noun.

uno.etymology: Uno continues Latin ūnus ('one, single'), supplying both the numeral uno/una and—through apocopated un before masculine singular nouns—the indefinite article.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: uno
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: un

uno.notes: Standalone 'one' stays uno (toma uno = take one), shortening to un directly before masculine nouns (un bollo).

usted.etymology: Usted contracted in Golden Age Spanish from the respectful courtly address vuestra merced ('Your Grace / Your Mercy'), through intermediate forms such as vusted.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: usted

usted.notes: That third-person noun origin ('Your Grace') explains why usted still takes third-person verb forms (usted tiene, ¿cómo está usted?) and possessive su!

ustedes.etymology: Ustedes is the regular plural of usted (< vuestras mercedes, 'Your Graces').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: usted

ustedes.notes: In Peninsula Spanish ustedes is reserved for polite/formal plural address (e.g. hotel guests), whereas in Canary Islands, parts of western Andalusia and all of Latin America ustedes is the universal plural 'you'.

veinte.etymology: Veinte descends from Latin vīgintī ('twenty') via Vulgar Latin *vīnti, with loss of voiced -g- and raising/diphthongization into Castilian veinte.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veinte

veinte.notes: Base of fused compounds veintiuno (21) through veintinueve (29).

veinticinco.etymology: Veinticinco fuses veinte (from Latin vīgintī, 'twenty') + y ('and') + cinco (through Vulgar Latin *cinque from Latin quīnque, 'five') into a single compound numeral.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veinticinco
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veinte
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cinco
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: cardinales

veinticinco.notes: Numbers from dieciséis (16) to veintinueve (29) are written as one word in Spanish, while treinta y uno (31) onward are written separately with y.

venir.etymology: Venir continues Latin venīre ('to come') with unchanged infinitive spelling.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: venir

venir.notes: Shares many stem patterns with tener: vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, venís, vienen; la semana que viene means 'next week'.

ventana.etymology: Ventana derives from Vulgar Latin *(fenestra) ventāna ('wind-opening', built on Latin ventus, 'wind'), uniquely replacing fenestra in Castilian and Portuguese.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ventana
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: viento

history.meaning: opening for wind and air -> window

ventana.notes: Notice how English 'window' ('wind-eye', from Old Norse vindauga) was coined from the exact same image of wind!

ver.etymology: Ver evolved from Old Spanish veer, continuing Latin vidēre ('to see') after regular loss of intervocalic -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ver

ver.notes: Retains the fuller stem ve- in veo ('I see'), veía (imperfect), and past participle visto; ¡A ver! means 'Let's see!'.

verdad.etymology: Verdad continues Latin verĭtas, veritātis ('truth', from vērus, 'true'), with syncope of unstressed -i- and voicing of -t- to -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: verdad

verdad.notes: ¿Verdad? at the end of a statement asks 'right? / isn't it?', and ¿De verdad? asks 'Really?'.

verde.etymology: Verde continues Vulgar Latin *virde, syncopated from Classical Latin virĭdis ('green, fresh, flourishing').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: verde

verde.notes: Two-form adjective: singular verde for both genders (el árbol verde, la farmacia verde), plural verdes.

viejo.etymology: Viejo descends from Vulgar Latin *veclus, syncopated from Classical Latin vetŭlus (diminutive of vetus, 'old'), with medial -cl- palatalizing to Old Spanish -j-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: viejo

viejo.notes: Placed before a noun (viejos amigos), viejo means 'long-standing' rather than elderly.

viernes.etymology: Viernes continues Latin (diēs) Venĕris ('day of Venus'), with stressed short ĕ diphthongizing to ie, metathesis of -nr- > -rn-, and analogical weekday -s.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: viernes

viernes.notes: Invariable in the plural: el viernes ('on Friday'), los viernes ('on Fridays').

vivir.etymology: Vivir continues Latin vīvēre ('to live, be alive, dwell'), shifting to the Spanish -ir conjugation.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vivir

volver.etymology: Volver continues Latin volvĕre ('to roll, turn around'), developing in Spanish into the primary verb for 'to return, come back'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: volver

volver.notes: Stem-changing o -> ue (vuelvo, vuelve) with past participle vuelto; volver a + infinitive is the idiomatic Spanish way to say 'do something again'.

vosotros.etymology: Vosotros fused Old Spanish vos ('you', from Latin vōs) + otros ('others', from Latin altĕrōs) in late medieval Castilian to mark plural informal 'you all' distinctly from singular respectful vos.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: vosotros

vosotros.notes: Everyday plural of tú across Peninsula Spain (feminine vosotras), paired with -áis / -éis / -ís verb endings and imperative -ad / -ed / -id (mirad, subid).

y.etymology: The conjunction y continues Latin et ('and'), which diphthongized in Old Spanish and reduced in unstressed position to a palatal vowel spelled y.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: y

y.notes: Before words beginning with an /i/ sound spelled i- or hi- (such as invierno or hijo), y changes to e to avoid repeating the same vowel sound.

ya.etymology: Ya descends regularly from Latin iam ('already, by now, right away'), with initial Latin i- palatalizing before a vowel into Castilian y-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ya

ya.notes: Depending on tense and tone, ya means 'already' (ya son las doce), 'now' (ya eres del equipo), or 'coming right away!' (¡Ya voy!).

yo.etymology: Yo comes through Vulgar Latin eo from Latin ego. The DLE groups it with the related case forms me and mí; modern Spanish uses yo when the speaker is the subject.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: yo

yo.notes: Yo can be omitted when the verb already identifies the speaker, or retained for contrast and emphasis.

éxito.etymology: Éxito comes as a learned borrowing from Latin exĭtus, meaning an going out, outcome or result. In modern Spanish the word narrowed specifically to a favourable outcome or success.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: éxito

éxito.notes: Watch out for the false friend with English 'exit': éxito means success, whereas a physical exit or departure is la salida.
